newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Striking Zimbabwe nurses defy ultimatum.
newsitem.headline: Striking Zimbabwe nurses defy ultimatum.

text.p: Thousands of Zimbabwean nurses forged ahead with a crippling strike for higher allowances but junior doctors went back to work on Wednesday after the government threatened to sack the strikers.

Police fired teargas to disperse the strikers when they marched to the Harare magistrate courts after scores of police officers barred them from a central city park where they have been assembling since they took to the streets on October 21.
Some 3,000 of the striking nurses then gathered outside Harare's main police station.
"We are not giving up the fight. The government must just give us what we are asking for," one of the strikers said.
State media reported that several patients around the country had died in the past week due to lack of attention as the strike by junior doctors and nurses dragged on.

On Tuesday night, acting Public Service, Labour and Social Welfare Minister Nathan Shamuyarira said: "Those who do not return to work on Wednesday will be dismissed forthwith and dismissed permanently. They will not be allowed to re-apply. The patience of government has run out."

A spokesman for the junior doctors, Farai Jiah, told reporters they were returning to their posts because they were tired of accusations by the government of President Robert Mugabe that they had persuaded the nurses to strike.

But they said they were just sitting around in the hospitals -- which are handling emergencies only with the help of army and Red Cross medical personnel -- because they could not work without the aid of nurses.
This is the second time in two months that the nurses and doctors have gone on strike for higher wages, allowances and negotiations on their conditions of service.

Last month they joined more than 100,000 civil servants -- including mortuary attendants, firefighters, immigration and customs officials -- in a three-week strike which paralysed essential social services.
The strike ended after the government awarded them a 20 percent pay rise and pledged to negotiate on their working conditions.
